despondent

/dih-SPON-duhnt/ - the stress falls on SPON · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Despondent means feeling depressed, discouraged, and hopeless.

The sidewalk portraitist grew despondent as a third straight rainy weekend washed out the art fair.

Example

The rescue center's manager stopped naming the January arrivals, and the volunteers understood before she said a word. Adoptions had stalled for a season; the kennels were full and the donation jar was not. Despondency at work looks like this — not tears but subtraction: no new names, shorter walks, paperwork done perfectly and nothing else attempted, a person conserving what little hope is left by spending none of it.

Despondent is the exact word for her, because it means feeling depressed, discouraged, and hopeless — and the third term carries the weight. Disappointment expects to try again; despondency has quietly stopped expecting. It sits lower than sad and quieter than desperate.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

dejected: Dejected is being cast down by one particular blow — a lost match, a botched audition — and it lifts as the blow fades. Despondent runs deeper: discouragement has hardened into hopelessness, and the person has quietly stopped expecting anything better.

downcast: Downcast is the sadness you can see — eyes lowered, shoulders slumped, a face gone quiet. It names the look, not the depth. Despondent names the depth: hope itself has drained away, whatever the face is doing.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

hopeful: still counting on a way through

lighthearted: carrying nothing heavy at all

Where it sits · how deep the loss of hope runs — disappointed → deflated → despondent

disappointed vs. despondent: Disappointed is the sting of one result — it fades by dessert and still expects to try again, which is exactly what despondent has stopped doing.

deflated vs. despondent: Deflated goes further than disappointed — the air has gone out of the whole effort for a while; despondent claims the most: hope itself has gone out, and trying feels beside the point.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — de-

Prefix — de-: away

Root — spond-

Root — spond-: to pledge (Latin spondere)

Suffix — -ent

Suffix — -ent: in a state of

Put it together

Put it together: De- (away) + spond- (to pledge) + -ent = having pledged away. Latin despondere meant to give up, to surrender — despondere animum, to sign one's spirit over. The same pledging root answers back in respond — to pledge in return — and stands guarantee in sponsor. A despondent person has, at the root's level, pledged their hope away.

Use the root in a new word: respond

Use the root in a new word: respond: Respond is re- + spond-: to pledge back — every answer is, at root, a small promise returned.

Word Choice

neutral / serious

Despondent describes people — and their letters, seasons, and locker rooms — never landscapes; hand those to this unit's desolate. Below it, deflated and dejected still have a pulse of intention; despondent has stopped dialing. It is a strong word: spend it where hope has actually gone missing, not on a rained-out picnic.
